content: The vaginal ecosystem is typically dominated by Lactobacillus species, along with other bacteria such as Megasphaera and Sneathia species, which help maintain a healthy balance until menopause. Bacterial vaginosis (BV) disrupts this balance and is associated with an increased risk of gynecological and obstetric complications, including preterm delivery, spontaneous abortion, and a higher likelihood of acquiring and transmitting HIV and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Gardnerella species play a central role in BV, as they adhere strongly to vaginal epithelial cells and initiate biofilm formation. These bacteria, along with Prevotella species, produce virulence factors like sialidases, which degrade the protective cervicovaginal mucus, facilitating biofilm formation and the attachment of other BV-associated bacteria. This process leads to the symptoms and signs of BV, including malodorous discharge caused by volatile amines produced by some bacteria. The loss of lactic acid-producing Lactobacilli results in an elevated vaginal pH, further contributing to the condition. Although BV is not classified as a sexually transmitted infection, evidence suggests that sexual transmission may play a role in its acquisition and recurrence. BV is linked to inconsistent condom use, new sexual partners, or an increased number of sexual partners, and its epidemiological profile aligns with that of an STI. Molecular data indicate that genital microbiota can be exchanged between sexual partners, with the penile and urethral microbiota of males often resembling the vaginal microbiota of their female partners. Men with a high prevalence of BV-associated bacteria on their penis are more likely to have female partners with confirmed BV. Male circumcision has been shown to reduce the prevalence of BV-associated bacteria in men and lower the risk of BV in their female partners. Clinically, approximately 90% of symptomatic women with BV report a white vaginal discharge, often accompanied by an abnormal vaginal odor. Some women may experience only mild discharge, which they might consider normal. On examination, a thin, white, homogeneous discharge may be observed on the vulva, particularly on the posterior fourchette or labia. During a speculum examination, the discharge may appear adherent to the vaginal walls, while the cervix typically appears normal. An amine odor, described as fishy, may be detected spontaneously or after adding a drop of 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) to vaginal fluid (the whiff test). However, recent sexual intercourse, douching, menstruation, or the use of antimicrobial agents can affect clinical and laboratory assessments for BV. Vaginal pH testing may yield inaccurate results if contaminated by water used for speculum lubrication or cervical secretions, which are relatively alkaline. Microscopic examination of vaginal fluid can aid in diagnosis. The presence of clue cells (vaginal epithelial cells coated with coccobacilli and lacking Lactobacilli rods) is a key diagnostic criterion for BV. Identifying clue cells requires adequate training and microscopy skills. Gram-stained vaginal smears may reveal large numbers of Gram-positive and Gram-negative coccobacilli with reduced or absent Lactobacilli. Diagnostic grading systems, such as the Ison-Hay criteria and Nugent’s score, are used to classify BV based on bacterial morphotypes. Nugent’s scoring system ranges from 0 to 10, with scores of 7–10 indicating BV, 4–6 suggesting intermediate microbiota, and 0–3 representing normal vaginal microbiota. Point-of-care tests, such as oligonucleotide probes for detecting high concentrations of Gardnerella species or tests for bacterial enzymes like sialidase, are available for BV diagnosis. Molecular assays based on RNA markers from Gardnerella and other anaerobic bacteria are also used. Treatment recommendations for BV include oral or intravaginal metronidazole, tinidazole, clindamycin, or secnidazole, with similar efficacy among these options. Intravaginal treatments and single-dose regimens may be preferred in cases where adherence to multiple doses is challenging. For anogenital warts caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), diagnosis is based on the presence of flat, papular, or pedunculated growths in the anogenital region. HPV-related cancers may present with abnormal bleeding, discharge, or non-healing lesions. HPV cannot be cultured conventionally, so molecular testing is used for epidemiological surveillance and clinical applications. Prophylactic HPV vaccines, which elicit strong immune responses, have proven safe and effective in preventing HPV-related infections and diseases, including cervical precancerous lesions and cancers. Vaccination is most effective before sexual debut but also benefits adults by reducing the risk of infection, genital warts, and anal canal disease. Cervical screening, traditionally performed using Pap smears or liquid-based cytology, remains a cornerstone of cervical cancer prevention. High-quality assurance and follow-up are essential for successful screening programs. HPV testing offers better specificity and allows for longer intervals between screenings for women who test negative. The effectiveness of HPV screening for preventing anal and oropharyngeal cancers is under evaluation. Treatment for external anogenital warts includes topical creams, cryotherapy, electrosurgery, or laser therapy. The choice of treatment depends on factors such as wart size, thickness, and anatomical location. Cryotherapy is considered the safest option during pregnancy. Prophylactic HPV vaccination has significantly reduced the incidence of genital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis caused by HPV types 6 and 11.
